name: Femi Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a tipper for the quarry outside town, the same quarry my dad drove for until his knees went. I load up under the hopper at seven, gravel or sand, take it out to building sites or the concrete plant, tip it, and come back for the next one, six or seven loads a day. I like that it's simple and I know every pothole on the quarry road. What wears me out is tipping on soft ground, because I'm still nervous the truck will lean, and the old boys can tell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the quarry?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years in March. Before that I did a bit of everything, labouring, a bar job. The pay's good for a junior and I don't spend much, so I've got about eleven months put away, and the car and my motorbike are paid for. My girlfriend Lena works at a bakery, so we're both up early, which suits us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, nothing to see. I'm not really online much, but in the canteen I'd say the clever people got excited over nothing again. Then we'd talk about the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, and that's all I want. The quarry has been there since before my dad was born. My worries would be the same as now, the soft ground and whether the quarry gets sold to a big firm that changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. I'd keep saving like I do, maybe put a bit toward a deposit with Lena. Maybe I'd ask the foreman to let me do more of the site tips so I get over my nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the one I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the quarry being sold. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's talk every year. A big building materials firm already bought the quarry over the hill, and they brought in all sorts of tablets and tracking. If the quarry gets sold, it won't be robots that change my job, it'll be some manager with a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of the routine work change, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the weighbridge does the tickets itself, which it half does already. I don't touch that, I just hand over the slip. My dad says the weighbridge man, Tony, has been there forty years, so I'd feel for him if it went.

say: I'd say the **clever people** got excited over **nothing** again.
I'd keep it to **canteen talk**, since I'm not online much.
think: I keep **my job**, which is all I want.
My real worries are **soft ground** and the quarry being **sold** to a big firm.
do: Carry on driving and **saving** as usual.
Put some savings toward a **deposit** with my girlfriend.
Ask for more **site tips** to get over my nerves.
feel: **Calm**, the picture he'd **choose** if he could.
S0.quote: If the quarry gets sold, it won't be robots that change my job, it'll be some manager with a spreadsheet.
fieldNote: His **family tie** to the quarry runs deep and shapes his sense of safety.
He fears a **takeover** more than technology.
He wants nothing to change and says so **plainly**.

steps.text: Keep hauling six or seven tipper loads a day
Ask the foreman for more site tips on soft ground
Put part of his savings toward a deposit with his girlfriend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem, not ours. You can't write an email that tips forty tonnes of sand. At the canteen I'd say let's wait and see before anyone panics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the videos of mines with trucks driving themselves on a closed road. A quarry is a closed road too, so I'm not as safe as I'm making out. If robots spread slowly, the quarry might still be one of the first places they show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do much, if I'm honest. I'd keep saving and probably put a bit more aside, maybe an extra hundred a month. I'm not going to learn computers, that's not me, so I'd just keep my head down and be the reliable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd pretend I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pretend. Who would you pretend to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, mainly, and my dad. My dad would get worked up and go on about the old days, and I don't want that. Lena would tell me to look at courses, and I don't want that either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the quarry is a closed road. What would that look like there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit inside the quarry, from the face to the hopper, is the easy part for a robot, same loop all day. The road out to the sites, with the roundabouts and the school run, is harder. So they'd probably take the quarry loop first, and I'm on the road, which helps a bit.

say: I'd say it's the **office people's** problem, not drivers'.
I'd tell the canteen to **wait and see** before panicking.
think: **Mines** already run self-driving trucks on **closed roads**, and a quarry is similar.
The quarry might be one of the **first places** robots show up.
do: Add an **extra hundred** a month to savings.
Keep my head down and be the **reliable** one.
S1.quote: You can't write an email that tips forty tonnes of sand.
fieldNote: There's a clear gap between his **public shrug** and his private worry about mines.
He'd **hide** his worry from his father and his girlfriend.
He reasons that **road work** is safer than the quarry loop.

steps.text: Put an extra hundred a month into savings
Wait to see if the quarry trials self-driving trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort something out for people like me, quick. I'm not a protest type, but I'd say it in the pub. And I'd say the companies should go slower, because nobody asked for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's bad for me. The office changes in 2028, then around 2031 the trucks drive themselves, and a quarry loop is the easiest job in the world for a robot. I'd be thirty-one, no qualifications, and the only thing I know is this tipper truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop spending on the bike and anything extra, and keep every penny I've saved. I'd ask my dad's friends if there's anything going that's hands-on and odd, like fixing machines. I'd probably still put off doing a course, because I wouldn't know which one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's a proper bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between 2028 and 2031 look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, but every day I'd wonder if this was the month. The bosses would be getting their AI to plan everything, and then one day there's a truck in the yard with no seat. I'd probably just keep turning up until they told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about eleven months saved. Does that change how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps, it means we don't lose the flat. But money isn't the job, is it? Eleven months of sitting at home would drive me mad, I need something to do with my hands.

say: I'd say the **government** needs to sort something out for people like me, fast.
I'd say companies should **slow down**, since nobody asked for this.
think: A **quarry loop** is the easiest job for a robot, around **2031**.
I'd be **thirty-one** with no qualifications, knowing only this truck.
do: Stop spending on the **motorbike** and extras.
Ask my dad's friends about **hands-on** jobs like fixing machines.
Delay choosing a **course** because I wouldn't know which.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one, no qualifications, and the only thing I know is this tipper truck.
fieldNote: He sees the **quarry loop** as the easiest target and expects to lose his job.
His **savings** ease the money fear but not the loss of purpose.
He'd keep **turning up** until told, rather than act early.

steps.text: Stop spending on the motorbike and nights out
Ask his dad's quarry friends about machine repair work
Keep driving until the quarry says the job is going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, so people should start sorting themselves out. I'd say it in the canteen more than anywhere. And I'd probably say the government ought to help with courses, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-four when the robot trucks come, around 2034. That's still young. But I know myself, I'd waste the first two years hoping it wouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and probably get the bigger licence for the eight-wheeler, because that's more pay while it lasts. Around year three I'd look at the fitter's course at the quarry workshop, fixing the machines instead of driving them. Lena would have to push me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there in the back of my head the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fitter's course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody has to fix the robot trucks when they break, and in a quarry they break a lot. Dust gets in everything. A fitter called Rob has been there twenty years and he's never short of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years. Why tell me that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's true. That's what I did after school, I waited for things to come to me. With five years, I'd probably wait two of them, and then panic for the other three.

say: I'd say **five years** is decent warning to sort yourself out.
I'd say the government should help with **courses**, though I doubt it.
think: I'd be **thirty-four** when robot trucks arrive, still young.
I'd likely **waste** the first two years hoping it won't happen.
do: Get the **bigger licence** for the eight-wheeler for more pay.
Look at the **fitter's course** at the quarry workshop in year three.
feel: **Anxious**, with the worry always at the back of his **head**.
S3.quote: Somebody has to fix the robot trucks when they break, and in a quarry they break a lot.
fieldNote: He is **honest** about his habit of waiting rather than acting.
Fixing robots in **dusty quarries** is a sharp and realistic idea.
He'd still need his **girlfriend** to push him to start.

steps.text: Get the eight-wheeler licence for higher tipper pay
Start the fitter's course at the quarry workshop in year three
Keep saving steadily from the quarry wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not get silly about it. Lots of things were meant to happen in ten years and didn't. I'd say that in the canteen and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, that's a problem for thirty-seven-year-old me. I'd be thirty-nine in 2039, so I'd have time to find something. The quarry would still need people for years, even if it's not driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, same as now. Maybe in five or six years I'd do the fitter's course, if the robot trucks are real by then. I'd buy a house with Lena and not change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier than five or six years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one. If a truck with no driver turned up at the quarry over the hill, I'd be on that fitter's course the next week. I believe things when I see them, not when someone on the news says them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad not to worry, I've got years. He'd say that's what they told the miners. Then he'd ask about the football, and that would be the end of it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, so nobody should get **silly** about it.
I'd point out that lots of things promised in a decade **never happened**.
think: It's a problem for **thirty-seven-year-old me**, with time to find something.
The quarry would still need **people** even without drivers.
do: Do the **fitter's course** in five or six years if robot trucks are real.
S4.quote: If a truck with no driver turned up at the quarry over the hill, I'd be on that fitter's course the next week.
fieldNote: He'd act only on **seeing proof**, not on news or forecasts.
His father's **miner comparison** sits underneath his confidence.
With a decade, he plans almost **no change**.

steps.text: Keep driving the tipper and saving as now
Wait for a driverless truck at a nearby quarry before retraining
Buy a house with his girlfriend in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a quarry is the easiest place for a robot truck, and I'd have no time and no plan. What would help is someone at the quarry telling us straight what's coming, and a course I could do at the workshop without giving up my wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would do all day. Money is one thing, but if you take away the tipper truck, what do lads like me do with ourselves? Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: Money is one thing, but if you take away the tipper truck, what do lads like me do with ourselves?
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** tipper driver at the quarry where his **father** drove before him.
He has about **eleven months** saved, a paid-off car and motorbike, and a girlfriend at a bakery.
He **avoids new tools** and admits he waits for things rather than acting early.
He fears the **quarry loop** is an easy target for robot trucks, and fixing machines is his fallback.
His mood runs from **calm** to **alarmed** in the fastest picture, settling to uneasy with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the quarry is an easy place for robot **trucks**.
whatWouldHelp: **Straight talk** from the quarry about what's coming.
A **workshop course** he could do without losing his wage.
